ety.text: Unknown. Attested since 1951 as US student slang. * Perhaps an alteration of nerts (“nuts", "crazy”); see references below. * The word, capitalized, appeared in 1950 in Dr. Seuss’s If I Ran the Zoo as the name of an imaginary animal: *: And then, just to show them, I’ll sail to Katroo / And bring back an It-Kutch, a Preep and a Proo, / A Nerkle, a Nerd and a Seersucker too! * Possibly a rebracketing of inert as a nert, as in he's inert = he's a nerd, in reference to one's lack of competence or athletic ability.

senses.d: A person who is intellectual but generally introverted.
ex: The bullies used to call him a nerd at school.
"We were all geeks and nerds, but he was unusually poorly adjusted," recalls Chess, now a mathematics professor at Hunter College.

senses.d: One who has an intense, obsessive interest in something.
ex: a computer nerd
a comic-book nerd

senses.d: A member of a subculture revolving around intellectualism, technology, video games, fantasy and science fiction, comic books and assorted media.
One who is stupid and socially inept or unattractive; a social outcast.
ex:
ALICE: Prithee , what might a nerd be ?
GLORIA: A nerd is an idiot or other person absurd.
To much of the world, we in America are nerds. We don't understand the world we live in.

From cerebro + -ito.
Unadapted borrowing from English nerd.
Abbreviation of cabeça-de-ferro (“iron head”), crânio-de-ferro (“iron skull”) or cu-de-ferro (“iron arse”).

Recorded since circa 1374 as Middle English nerve, from Medieval Latin nervus (“nerve”), from Latin nervus (“sinew”). Doublet of neuron and sinew. Verb sense 4 (“to get on (someone’s) nerves”) is chiefly a semantic loan from German nerven.

senses.d: A bundle of neurons with their connective tissue sheaths, blood vessels and lymphatics.
ex: The nerves can be seen through the skin.

Like her I go; I cannot stay;
⁠I leave this mortal ark behind,
A weight of nerves without a mind,
And leave the cliffs, and haste away […]

senses.d: A neuron.
A vein in a leaf; a grain in wood.
ex: Some plants have ornamental value because of their contrasting nerves.

senses.d: Courage; boldness; audacity; gall.
ex: He had the nerve to enter my house uninvited.
He hasn't the nerve to tell her he likes her.

senses.d: Patience; stamina; endurance, fortitude.
ex: The web-team found git-sed is really a time and nerve saver when doing mass changes on your repositories
He led me on to mightiest deeds, / Above the nerve of mortal arm.

senses.d: One's neural structures considered collectively as, and conceptually equated with, one's psyche.
ex: All these rationalizations for asinine behavior are getting on my nerves.
His nerves could no longer handle the worry.

senses.d: Mental agitation caused by fear, stress or other negative emotions.
ex: Ellie had a bad case of nerves before the big test; she was a bundle of nerves.
Put me in the hospital for nerves and then they had to commit me

senses.d: The elastic resistance of raw rubber or other polymers to permanent deformation during processing.
Sinew, tendon.
ex: Come on; obey: / Thy nerves are in their infancy again, / And have no vigour in them.

senses.d: A particular simplicial set constructed from a category.
To give courage.
ex: May their example nerve us to face the enemy.
And how I strained my ears, and nerved my hands and limbs, beginning to twitch with convulsive movements, which I feared might betray me!

senses.d: To give strength; to supply energy or vigour.
ex: The liquor nerved up several of the men after their icy march.

senses.d: To perform a neurectomy on (someone or something).
ex: You can't nerve a hoof and I didn't realize that the cannon bone where the nerving takes place is not part of the leg.
Her instructor was trying to convince me that her horse's tail "needed" to be nerved.

senses.d: To get on (someone’s) nerves; to annoy, irritate, or bother (someone).
ex: Do not nerve others: Of course it helps to talk to others. But just when you've got a lot of information, that can be annoying.

senses.d: To be nervous.
ex: use the extrapolar solution, don't nerve.
Broadband Quality :) Stop nerving!!!

Proto-Indo-European *preyskosder. Proto-Germanic *friskazbor. Vulgar Latin *friscum Spanish fresco Proto-Indo-European *-tew-? Proto-Indo-European *-r-eh₂? Classical Latin -tūra Latin -ūra Spanish -ura Spanish frescura From fresco + -ura.
Learned borrowing from Latin patientia, derived from patiēns, present active participle of patior (“to suffer”).

From Middle English nervous (“composed of or incorporating nerves”), from Latin nervōsus (“nervous; sinewy; energetic, vigorous”), from nervus (“nerve; muscle; sinew, tendon; (figuratively) energy, power; nerve; force, strength, vigour”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snéh₁wr̥ (“sinew, tendon”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns). The English word is analysable as nerve + -ous.

senses.d: Full of sinews.
Having strong or prominent sinews; sinewy, muscular.
Of a piece of writing, literary style etc.: forceful, powerful.
ex: Fortescutus illustratus, or a commentary on that nervous treatise De Laudibus Legum Angliæ […] [book title]
Nervous, clear, and striking, was almost all that he uttered […].

senses.d: Supplied with nerves; innervated.
Affecting or involving the nerves or nervous system.
Nervose.
ex: CANNACORUS, […] It hath a knobbed tuberoſe Root: The Leaves are long and nervous: […]

senses.d: Easily agitated or alarmed; edgy, on edge.
ex: Being in a crowd of strangers makes me nervous.

senses.d: Apprehensive, anxious, hesitant, worried.
